title: Bronchiectasis: Chronic Sputum, Exacerbations, and Airway Clearance
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic airway dilation with impaired mucus clearance, recurrent infection/exacerbations and sometimes hemoptysis. Confirm structurally with chest CT, look for an underlying cause, obtain sputum microbiology when clinically useful, and make airway clearance plus exacerbation prevention the centre of long-term care.
recognize: Chronic productive cough, daily sputum, recurrent lower-respiratory infections and hemoptysis are common clues.
Frequent exacerbations, weight loss, clubbing or unusual organisms raise severity and underlying-cause concerns.
differentiate: COPD/chronic bronchitis can produce chronic sputum without established bronchiectasis; high-resolution CT demonstrates bronchial dilation and related changes.
Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary disorders, immune deficiency, ABPA, aspiration and prior severe infection can cause bronchiectasis and change management.
assessment: Assess exacerbation frequency, sputum volume/colour, hemoptysis, dyspnea, lung function, oxygenation, prior cultures, aspiration/reflux, sinus disease, immune history and vaccination.
workup: Use chest CT for structural confirmation; obtain sputum culture during clinically significant exacerbation and evaluate underlying causes according to age/history/severity.
Pulmonary function testing helps characterize airflow limitation but does not diagnose bronchiectasis by itself.
management: Teach individualized airway-clearance therapy and exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation where appropriate; treat exacerbations using prior/current microbiology and local guidance, and address chronic colonization or frequent exacerbations with respiratory-specialist input.
Manage the cause and comorbid asthma/COPD when present rather than prescribing chronic antibiotics reflexively.
medicationSafety: Repeated broad-spectrum antibiotics increase resistance and C. difficile risk; inhaled or long-term macrolide strategies require specialist selection and monitoring.
Bronchodilators are useful when reversible/obstructive physiology or symptomatic benefit is present, not simply because CT shows bronchiectasis.
redFlags: Unexplained weight loss or focal obstruction
counselling: Teach airway-clearance technique, hydration/exercise as appropriate, vaccination, sputum-change action plan and when hemoptysis or breathlessness requires urgent care.
followUp: Track exacerbations, cultures, lung function, symptoms and treatment burden; refer persistent/frequent disease to respiratory care.
examTrap: Treating every chronic productive cough as COPD or repeatedly prescribing antibiotics without confirming bronchiectasis and reviewing airway clearance/cultures.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is clearance plus culture-informed exacerbation management plus a search for why the airways became damaged.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Non-CF Bronchiectasis clinical practice resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension: Recognize the Syndrome and Refer the Right Cause
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes. Unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope, right-heart failure or suggestive echocardiography should trigger structured evaluation and specialist referral; do not start pulmonary arterial hypertension drugs from an echo estimate alone.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest discomfort, presyncope/syncope, loud P2, RV heave, edema or elevated JVP can occur.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension is a treatable cause that must be considered after PE or unexplained pulmonary hypertension.
differentiate: Pulmonary hypertension from left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia, chronic thromboemboli and pulmonary arterial hypertension have different treatment pathways.
Echocardiography estimates probability and RV consequences; right-heart catheterization is the definitive hemodynamic test for many treatment decisions.
assessment: Assess dyspnea trajectory, syncope, VTE history, connective-tissue disease, HIV/liver disease, appetite/weight-loss drugs or stimulants, sleep/lung disease, pregnancy and signs of RV failure.
workup: Use ECG/chest imaging, echocardiography, PFTs, oxygenation and cause-directed labs; evaluate chronic thromboembolic disease with the appropriate imaging pathway and refer for definitive hemodynamic assessment when probability is significant.
management: Treat the underlying cause, oxygen/hypoxemia and volume overload as appropriate, and refer suspected PAH/CTEPH or unexplained significant pulmonary hypertension to expert care.
Pregnancy in significant pulmonary hypertension requires high-risk specialist management.
medicationSafety: Pulmonary vasodilators used for PAH can be inappropriate or harmful in other pulmonary-hypertension groups; do not prescribe empirically from an echo report.
Diuretics require renal/electrolyte and preload assessment in right-heart failure.
counselling: Explain why pulmonary hypertension is a category requiring cause classification rather than one medication diagnosis.
followUp: Ensure specialist workup is closed-loop and track RV function, symptoms, oxygenation and precipitating disease.
examTrap: Starting a PAH-specific vasodilator because echocardiography estimates elevated pulmonary pressure before defining the pulmonary-hypertension group.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is a syndrome first; the cause determines the therapy.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary vascular disease guidance
Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Thoracic Society pulmonary hypertension position resources

title: Sarcoidosis: Compatible Pattern, Exclude Mimics, Assess Organs
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis built from a compatible clinical/radiographic pattern, histology when required, and exclusion of important mimics such as infection or malignancy. Treatment is driven by organ threat and functional impairment, not the presence of granulomas alone.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, cough/dyspnea, erythema nodosum, uveitis and systemic symptoms are common patterns.
Cardiac, neurologic, ocular or significant hypercalcemia involvement can be disproportionately dangerous even when lung symptoms are mild.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, drug reactions and occupational/environmental granulomatous disease can mimic sarcoidosis.
Not every radiographic stage requires corticosteroid treatment; asymptomatic stable disease may be observed.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms/function, skin/eye symptoms, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, calcium/kidney history, exposures, TB/fungal risk and medications.
workup: Use chest imaging, PFTs, CBC/chemistry/calcium and organ-directed testing; obtain tissue when diagnosis is uncertain or needed before treatment, choosing the safest/highest-yield site.
Screen for ocular/cardiac involvement based on current specialty practice and symptoms.
management: Observe stable low-risk disease when appropriate; use corticosteroids or steroid-sparing immunosuppression for organ-threatening or functionally significant disease with specialist coordination.
medicationSafety: Immunosuppression requires infection screening and toxicity monitoring; avoid treating presumed sarcoid before excluding infection when clinical context makes that plausible.
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can affect more than the lungs and that treatment intensity depends on which organs are involved.
followUp: Track symptoms, PFT/imaging and involved-organ function; persistent or complex disease warrants respiratory/multidisciplinary follow-up.
examTrap: Starting prolonged steroids for bilateral hilar adenopathy before excluding tuberculosis or another granulomatous mimic.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis is compatible granulomatous disease after the dangerous mimics are excluded—and organ risk decides whether to treat.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian respiratory specialty practice resources

title: Adult Cystic Fibrosis: Multisystem Care Through a CF Centre
bottomLine: Adult cystic fibrosis is a complex multisystem disease requiring coordinated CF-centre care. Primary/acute-care NPs should recognize pulmonary exacerbation, maintain infection-control and medication continuity, identify CFRD/liver/bone/nutrition/reproductive issues, and involve the CF team early rather than simplifying care to 'chronic lung infection'.
recognize: Chronic airway infection/bronchiectasis, declining spirometry, increased cough/sputum, weight loss and reduced exercise tolerance can signal pulmonary exacerbation.
CF-related diabetes, pancreatic insufficiency, liver disease, bone disease, sinus disease and fertility/reproductive issues are major adult-care domains.
differentiate: CF pulmonary exacerbation can occur without dramatic fever or radiographic change; compare symptoms and lung function with personal baseline.
CFTR modulator eligibility and regimen are genotype/product-specific and managed with the CF team.
assessment: Assess baseline FEV1, sputum organisms, airway-clearance regimen, inhaled/systemic antibiotics, CFTR modulators, nutrition/enzymes, diabetes, liver/bone health, pregnancy plans and mental health.
workup: Use sputum microbiology, spirometry and targeted imaging/labs during suspected exacerbation; screen/manage multisystem complications according to Canadian CF-centre guidelines.
management: Continue airway-clearance/chronic therapies unless contraindicated, treat exacerbations based on severity and prior organisms with CF-team input, and protect nutrition/hydration.
Coordinate CFTR-modulator, antimicrobial and complication management through an accredited CF program.
medicationSafety: Drug interactions, liver monitoring and pregnancy considerations may be important for CFTR modulators; aminoglycosides and other antibiotics can require renal/level monitoring.
Cross-infection precautions between people with CF are important in clinical environments.
counselling: Support transition/self-management, airway-clearance adherence, reproductive planning and mental-health care without making the patient re-teach the whole CF regimen at every encounter.
followUp: Ensure any acute-care changes are communicated back to the CF centre and chronic complications remain under coordinated surveillance.
examTrap: Treating an adult CF pulmonary exacerbation like routine community-acquired pneumonia without reviewing prior organisms, baseline lung function, airway clearance and CF-team plan.
oneLinePearl: Adult CF is multidisciplinary chronic disease; acute respiratory care must stay connected to the CF centre.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada Canadian Guidelines for CF Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada Standards of Care

title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Differential Early
bottomLine: An immunocompromised patient with respiratory symptoms can deteriorate quickly and may have muted fever or atypical imaging. Define the immune defect, severity and exposure, consider opportunistic as well as routine pathogens, obtain appropriate microbiology promptly and escalate hypoxemia or neutropenic infection early.
recognize: Neutropenia, transplant, hematologic malignancy, high-dose/prolonged corticosteroids and biologic/targeted immune therapies create different pathogen risks.
Pneumocystis, fungal, mycobacterial, viral and resistant bacterial infections may present with nonspecific cough/dyspnea or subtle fever.
differentiate: Drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, malignancy progression, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and pulmonary embolism can mimic infection.
A normal initial chest X-ray does not reliably exclude early opportunistic pneumonia in a high-risk host.
assessment: Assess immune condition/medications, neutrophil count, transplant timing, prophylaxis, exposures/travel, oxygenation, hemodynamics and prior microbiology.
workup: Use CBC/differential, cultures/molecular testing and chest CT or bronchoscopy when severity/risk warrants; select opportunistic testing from the specific immune defect rather than ordering every test.
management: Escalate unstable, hypoxemic or neutropenic patients to acute specialist care; initiate empiric therapy when delay is dangerous while pursuing definitive microbiology and alternative diagnoses.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic dysfunction and major drug interactions can change antimicrobial choice; prophylaxis history does not eliminate breakthrough infection.
counselling: Teach patients on significant immunosuppression to seek early assessment for new dyspnea/fever rather than waiting for classic pneumonia symptoms.
followUp: Close microbiology and antimicrobial-narrowing decisions and coordinate with oncology/transplant/infectious-disease teams.
examTrap: Reassuring a neutropenic patient with dyspnea because there is no fever or the first chest X-ray is normal.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, absence of classic inflammation is not absence of serious infection.
sourceBasis: Canadian antimicrobial stewardship and immunocompromised-host practice principles

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Prescribe the Target
bottomLine: Oxygen is a drug used to treat hypoxemia, not dyspnea by itself. Prescribe a target saturation/range and delivery system appropriate to the disease, reassess response and ventilation, and distinguish short-term acute oxygen from evidence-based long-term home oxygen qualification.
recognize: Hypoxemia, respiratory distress and acute organ-threatening illness may require immediate supplemental oxygen while the cause is treated.
Patients at risk of chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure need controlled oxygen plus ventilation assessment rather than indiscriminate high-flow oxygen.
differentiate: A breathless but normoxemic patient may need bronchodilation, diuresis, ventilatory support or cause-specific therapy—not oxygen.
Long-term home oxygen requires documented chronic hypoxemia criteria and reassessment; it is not prescribed simply for exertional fatigue or patient preference.
assessment: Assess SpO2 quality/trend, work of breathing, mental status, perfusion, ABG/VBG when ventilation matters, baseline lung disease and exertional/sleep context.
workup: Investigate the cause of hypoxemia; use arterial oxygen assessment/home-oxygen qualification testing according to local Canadian respiratory program criteria.
management: Titrate oxygen to the clinical target while treating the cause; escalate to noninvasive/invasive ventilatory support when oxygenation or ventilation cannot be maintained safely.
medicationSafety: Excess oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients and can create absorption/oxidative risks; the solution is controlled titration and ventilation assessment, not withholding oxygen from severe hypoxemia.
counselling: For home oxygen, teach fire/smoking safety, equipment use and that flow changes should follow the prescribed plan.
followUp: Reassess oxygen need after acute illness and periodically for home therapy; remove unnecessary oxygen when criteria are no longer met.
examTrap: Giving oxygen to every dyspneic patient while ignoring normal saturation—or withholding oxygen from severe hypoxemia because of fear of CO2 retention.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen treats low oxygen; ventilation support treats inadequate CO2 clearance.

title: Mechanical Ventilation: Oxygenation, Ventilation, and Lung Protection
bottomLine: Mechanical ventilation is supportive therapy while the cause of respiratory failure is treated. Separate oxygenation problems from ventilation problems, use lung-protective principles when indicated, monitor synchrony/hemodynamics and identify immediately reversible ventilator emergencies before changing multiple settings blindly.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP primarily influence oxygenation; minute ventilation/tidal volume/rate influence CO2 clearance, though all settings interact with lung mechanics.
High airway pressures can reflect resistance, low compliance, coughing, tube problems, pneumothorax or patient-ventilator dyssynchrony.
differentiate: A high peak pressure with relatively normal plateau suggests resistance; high plateau suggests reduced compliance/overdistension when measured correctly.
Hypoxemia after intubation can be equipment/tube, lung or circulation related—check the patient and circuit before reflex escalation.
assessment: Assess airway/tube position, chest rise/breath sounds, SpO2/ETCO2/gases, BP/perfusion, sedation/synchrony, secretions and ventilator pressures/alarms.
workup: Use blood gas and imaging/ultrasound as clinically needed; evaluate sudden deterioration with a structured tube/circuit/pneumothorax/secretions/hemodynamics approach.
management: Use lung-protective tidal-volume/pressure strategies for ARDS and appropriate PEEP/FiO2 titration; optimize analgesia/sedation and treat the underlying cause.
Weaning requires improving cause, oxygenation/ventilation, hemodynamic stability and ability to protect the airway.
medicationSafety: Sedation/neuromuscular blockade can cause hypotension/delirium/weakness and must be titrated to indication; avoid assuming agitation always needs more sedation before checking pain, hypoxemia, tube/circuit and delirium.
redFlags: High-pressure alarm with unilateral breath sounds
counselling: When appropriate, explain that the ventilator supports breathing while the underlying illness is treated and that settings change as physiology changes.
followUp: Reassess gases, pressures, hemodynamics and readiness to reduce support; document cause-specific ventilation goals.
examTrap: Turning up FiO2 for rising CO2 or increasing sedation for every ventilator alarm without assessing the patient and circuit.
oneLinePearl: On a ventilator, first decide whether the problem is oxygenation, ventilation, mechanics, equipment or the underlying disease.

title: Asthma-COPD Overlap: Protect Against Asthma Risk While Treating Fixed Obstruction
bottomLine: Patients can have persistent airflow obstruction plus asthma features. When asthma is genuinely present, controller therapy must include inhaled corticosteroid rather than LABA monotherapy; then add long-acting bronchodilation and risk-factor/exacerbation management according to the COPD component.
recognize: Asthma clues include variable symptoms, atopy/early onset and significant reversibility; COPD clues include persistent obstruction, smoking/biomass exposure and progressive exertional limitation.
Do not create an 'overlap' label merely because an older smoker wheezes—confirm spirometry and historical phenotype.
differentiate: Asthma and COPD have different risk implications: asthma makes LABA monotherapy unsafe, while COPD often requires stronger long-acting bronchodilation and exacerbation prevention.
assessment: Assess symptom variability, exacerbations/hospitalization, smoking/exposure, eosinophilic/atopic features, inhaler technique/adherence, pneumonia risk and spirometry.
workup: Confirm persistent airflow obstruction with spirometry after bronchodilator and assess reversibility/phenotype without expecting one threshold to perfectly distinguish asthma from COPD.
management: If asthma is present, ensure ICS-containing therapy; add LABA/LAMA according to persistent symptoms/exacerbations and COPD guidance, plus smoking cessation, vaccination and pulmonary rehab when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Avoid LABA monotherapy in asthma; use the lowest effective ICS exposure consistent with asthma control while considering pneumonia/side-effect risk in COPD-predominant disease.
counselling: Explain why inhalers have different jobs and confirm device technique rather than escalating doses around poor delivery.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, rescue use, spirometry and adverse effects; re-evaluate the phenotype when treatment response is unexpected.
examTrap: Treating fixed obstruction plus clear asthma history with LABA alone—or diagnosing overlap without spirometry/phenotype evidence.
oneLinePearl: When asthma is truly part of the picture, protect the patient with ICS-containing therapy; then manage the COPD burden too.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society COPD pharmacotherapy guidance
